title: RV Recycling: What Actually Gets Recycled
metaDescription: RV recycling typically salvages metal, appliances, tires, batteries, and some interior components, while fiberglass bodies and non‑recyclable parts often end up in a landfill or specialized scrap facility.
body:
META: RV recycling typically salvages metal, appliances, tires, batteries, and some interior components, while fiberglass bodies and non‑recyclable parts often end up in a landfill or specialized scrap facility. KEYWORDS: rv recycling, rv scrap metal, rv disposal, junk removal pricing, how to recycle an rv # RV Recycling: What Actually Gets Recycled When you recycle an RV, **the metal frame, engine, transmission, wheels, tires, batteries, appliances, and any recyclable interior fixtures are recovered**, while the fiberglass shell, foam insulation, and non‑recyclable plastics usually go to a landfill or a specialty scrap yard. Below is a step‑by‑step guide that starts with the cheapest, most environmentally friendly options and ends with paid junk‑removal services when you need a hand. --- ## 1. Transfer Ownership & Legal Clean‑Up ### 1.1 Cancel the Title and License Plates * **DMV notification** – Submit a Notice of Transfer and Release of Liability. * **Remove plates** – Return them to the DMV or destroy them per state rules. ### 1.2 Check for Outstanding Loans or Liens * Pay off any remaining balance or arrange a payoff‑by‑sale with the lender. ### 1.3 Document the Condition * Take photos and note mileage; this helps when you negotiate with salvage yards or donors. --- ## 2. Donate or Sell Usable Parts First ### 2.1 Donation Programs * **Habitat for Humanity ReStore**, **Goodwill**, and local **Veterans’ charities** accept RVs that are still drivable or can be stripped for parts. * You may receive a **tax deduction** (consult a tax professional). ### 2.2 Private Sale of Components * **Engine, transmission, and axles** can fetch $200‑$800 each depending on condition. * **Appliances** (refrigerator, stove, microwave) often sell for **$50‑$150** each on Craigslist or Facebook Marketplace. ### 2.3 Why This Saves Money * Removing high‑value items reduces the volume you’ll need to haul, lowering any later removal cost by up to **30 %**. --- ## 3. Scrap Metal & Component Recycling ### 3.1 What Metal Gets Recycled | Component | Typical Material | Approx. Weight | Typical Recycling Value* | |-----------|------------------|----------------|--------------------------| | Frame & chassis | Steel | 800‑1,200 lb | $0.05‑$0.15 / lb | | Engine & transmission | Cast iron/steel | 400‑600 lb | $0.07‑$0.20 / lb | | Wheels & rims | Steel/aluminum | 150‑250 lb | $0.04‑$0.12 / lb | | Tubular steel (tanks, supports) | Steel | 100‑200 lb | $0.05‑$0.15 / lb | | Batteries (lead‑acid) | Lead | 30‑50 lb each | $0.30‑$0.50 / lb (often paid to take) | \*Values vary by region; urban centers with higher landfill fees pay more for scrap. ### 3.2 Where to Take It * **Local scrap yards** – Call ahead for weight‑based tipping fees (often **$30‑$60 per ton**). * **Specialty RV recyclers** – Some accept whole units, dismantle on‑site, and pay for metal. ### 3.3 How to Prepare * Drain all fluids (fuel, oil, refrigerant). * Remove batteries and label them as hazardous. * Separate aluminum wheels from steel rims for higher pay. --- ## 4. Handling Non‑Recyclable Materials ### 4.1 Fiberglass Shells * Most landfills **do not accept fiberglass**; you need a **specialty demolition contractor**. * Expect a **disposal fee of $300‑$600** for a full‑size RV shell. ### 4.2 Foam Insulation & Plastic Trim * Typically **landfilled**; some recycling centers accept bulk foam for **$0.02‑$0.04 / lb**. ### 4.3 Propane Tanks & Hazardous Waste * **Empty and return** the tank to a retailer for a **$5‑$10** refund. * Any residual refrigerant must be reclaimed by a licensed technician. --- ## 5. DIY vs. Professional Junk Removal ### 5.1 When DIY Makes Sense * You have a **truck or trailer** that can handle the load. * You can **strip and separate** metal, appliances, and tires yourself. * You live near a **scrap yard with low tipping fees**. ### 5.2 When to Call a Pro * The RV is **immobile**, too large for your vehicle, or located on a **tight lot**. * You lack the time or equipment to **drain fluids** safely. * You prefer a **single‑day, all‑in‑one service** that handles permits, loading, and cleanup. #### 5.2.1 1‑800‑GOT‑JUNK Overview * **Pricing** is volume‑based in 1/8‑truck increments. * Minimum load (1/8 truck, 1.25 ft × 5 ft × 8 ft) costs **$100‑$150**. * Small loads range **$107‑$396**. * Medium loads **$396‑$600**. * Large loads **$600‑$1,099**. * **What’s included** – labor, loading from anywhere on the property, hauling, disposal/recycling fees, and post‑job cleanup. Crews are licensed and insured. * **Booking** – free on‑site estimate (no credit card required), crew calls 25‑30 min before arrival, same‑day service often available. * **Discount truth** – No official military, senior, student, or AAA discounts. Email‑list sign‑ups can net **$10‑$25** off; local franchise promos may apply. #### 5.2.2 Competitor Snapshot | Company | Minimum Charge | Pricing Model | Typical Range (Volume) | Notable Fees | |---------|----------------|---------------|------------------------|--------------| | **1‑800‑GOT‑JUNK** | $100‑$150 (1/8 truck) | Volume‑based | $107‑$1,099 | Mattress recycling fee $10.50 in CA/CT/RI | | **LoadUp** | $89 minimum | Per‑item, fixed online price | $89‑$600+ (depends on items) | No hidden fees; price locked at booking | | **Junk King** | $99 minimum | Volume‑based | $389‑$488 (half truck)
$589‑$658 (full truck) | Approx. online estimate | | **College Hunks** | $150‑$750 per job | Volume‑based | $150‑$750 | $99 service/dispatch fee disclosed after booking | ### 5.3 Worked Dollar Example You have a **medium‑size RV** (≈ 12 ft long, 5 ft high, 8 ft wide) that you’ve stripped of appliances and batteries. The remaining shell weighs about **2,500 lb** (≈ 1.25 tons). 1. **Scrap metal value** (average $0.10 / lb) → **$250** paid by the scrap yard. 2. **Tire disposal fee** – 4 tires @ $15 each → **$60**. 3. **Fiberglass disposal** – specialist quote **$450**. **Total cost without a pro service:** *Disposal fees* = $60 + $450 = **$510** *Net after scrap credit* = $510 – $250 = **$260** If you hired **1‑800‑GOT‑JUNK** for a **medium load** (price $500 average), you’d pay **$500** and receive no scrap credit. The DIY route saves about **$240** but requires a truck, time, and handling of hazardous fluids. --- ## 6. Common Mistakes & How to Avoid Them | Mistake | Why It Hurts | Fix | |---------|--------------|-----| | **Leaving fluids in the RV** | Illegal dumping fines; hazardous waste fees can add $200‑$400. | Drain fuel, oil, coolant, and refrigerant before transport. | | **Trying to haul the whole RV on a small trailer** | Over‑loading can damage your vehicle and cause safety violations. | Split the job: remove shell, metal, and tires separately. | | **Assuming the entire RV is recyclable** | Fiberglass, foam, and some plastics are not accepted at most yards. | Research local facilities; budget for non‑recyclable disposal. | | **Not checking for local scrap yard tipping fees** | You might pay $300 for a load that could be $150 elsewhere. | Call 2‑3 yards for per‑ton rates before committing. | | **Relying on outdated coupon codes** | Most codes are invalid; you waste time and may miss real savings. | Join the 1‑800‑GOT‑JUNK email list for verified $10‑$25 discounts. | | **Skipping the donation step** | You lose potential tax deductions and free removal by charities. | List usable parts on free platforms before scrapping the rest. | --- ## 7. Frequently Asked Questions **Q1: Can I recycle the entire RV in one trip?** A: Only if you have a **full‑size flatbed truck** and a local scrap yard that accepts whole units. Most owners need to dismantle it into smaller components. **Q2: How much is a mattress recycling fee?** A: In California, Connecticut, and Rhode Island the **Bye Bye Mattress** program adds a **$10.50 per unit** fee, which 1‑800‑GOT‑JUNK may pass through. **Q3: Do I need a permit to dump an RV?** A: Many municipalities require a **disposal permit** for large items. Check your city’s public works website; the permit cost is usually **$20‑$50**. **Q4: What’s the best way to get cash for scrap metal?** A: Call several local scrap yards for **weight‑based rates**, bring a **scale‑ticket** if possible, and negotiate the highest per‑pound price. Some yards pay extra for clean, separated metal. **Q5: Are there any free recycling programs for RV tires?** A: Some **state environmental agencies** run tire‑recycling events or offer **$5‑$10 per tire** credits. Search “tire recycling program + [your state]”. **Q6: How does the “Flex” product from 1‑800‑GOT‑JUNK work?** A: You load a bag or container yourself, then the crew picks it up for a flat fee starting at **$39**. It’s useful for small items like mattresses or a single sofa, but not for an entire RV. --- ## Takeaway **Recycle the metal, batteries, and appliances yourself whenever possible; use a scrap yard for the shell and pay only the necessary disposal fees.** Paid junk‑removal services like 1‑800‑GOT‑JUNK are convenient but typically cost more than a DIY approach once you factor in scrap credits. --- [CTA]
